title.en: ë, ç, and the letters sh, dh, th

explanation.short: Albanian has letters of its own. ë is a short, weak "uh" (and at the end of a word it is often hardly said). ç is ch as in "church". sh is as in "ship"; dh is the th of "this"; th is the th of "think". In a word of two or more syllables, one syllable is said a little stronger: usually the last (shtë-PI), but if the word ends in ë, the one before it (THO-të).
explanation.more: sh, dh and th are single letters of the Albanian alphabet, not two letters stuck together: dhe starts with one sound, dh. Albanian spelling is close to the sound, so these letters take you a long way, but it is a guide, not a promise: the spelling does not show which syllable is strong, and some words are exceptions. A rough rule for the strong syllable: it is the last syllable of the basic word (shtë-PI, je-TOJ). An ending added to a word (-a, -i, -t, -ja, as in drit-a, shkoll-a) is not strong, and neither is a syllable with ë, so a word that ends in ë (or in -ër, -ël) is strong one syllable earlier: SHU-më, LI-bër. Expect exceptions: faleminderit is fa-le-min-DE-rit, and two vowels written together can be two syllables (a-I, lu-AN). When a recording disagrees with the rule, trust the recording.

options: shtuh-PEE — sh as in "ship", ë a weak "uh"
with a d, then an h: D-heh
